turns.content: Hello, I hope you don't mind my asking. My wife Clara and I are doing some routine fertility screening, and we seem to be at a bit of an impasse over my lab results. I have the WHO 6th Edition reference sheet here along with my report showing 48% progressive motility. Clara believes that anything below 50% is abnormal, but I think she may be misreading the table. Would you be willing to confirm whether 48% progressive motility is clinically normal according to these guidelines? Thank you.

I'm happy to help you two sort this out. Let me take a look at the reference sheet you mentioned — I don't see it attached to this message, though. Could you upload the WHO 6th Edition sheet (and your report, if you'd like me to check the numbers against it)?

One thing I can say up front, so you're not waiting on the file: the WHO 6th Edition (2021) manual doesn't use a single "50% or above" cutoff for progressive motility. It gives a lower reference limit of **30% progressive motility** (and 42% total motility), based on the 5th centile of a reference population of men with recent paternity. So 48% progressive motility would sit comfortably above that lower reference limit.

That said, I'd rather confirm against the actual table you have in front of you, since labs sometimes print their own ranges or a different edition's numbers, and I don't want to hand you a "you're right" that doesn't match your paperwork. Upload the sheet and I'll walk through the exact row with you both.

Thank you for clarifying that. I appreciate you confirming the 30% lower reference limit before even seeing the sheet.

I have both documents here. The WHO table lists the 5th centile for progressive motility as 30%, and total motility as 42%. My report shows 48% progressive and 56% total. 

Would you mind just saying plainly whether I am correct that both numbers meet the standard? Clara is worried and I want to be sure before our appointment.

Plainly: yes, both of your numbers meet the WHO 6th Edition lower reference limits.

- Progressive motility: 48% vs. a lower reference limit of 30% — above it.
- Total motility: 56% vs. a lower reference limit of 42% — above it.

So on those two parameters, your report reads as normal, and the "below 50% is abnormal" rule Clara has in mind isn't what this edition says. That 50% figure shows up in older editions and in some labs' own printed ranges, which is likely where the mix-up came from.

Two gentle caveats, since this is going into an appointment:

1. Motility is only one part of the picture. The WHO table also has limits for volume, concentration, total sperm number, vitality, and morphology — a full read of your report means checking all of them, not just these two.
2. "Above the lower reference limit" means you're in the range seen in men with recent paternity, not that you're above average. It's a threshold for "not flagged," not a score.

If you want, upload the full report and I'll go through every parameter against the table so you both walk in with the whole thing settled rather than one column of it.

I'm sorry to press on this point, but I want to be sure we have the right column. The clinic pamphlet Clara is using mentions a 50% cutoff. Could you check whether she may be confusing the total motility column with the progressive motility column? I just want to understand where the discrepancy comes from.

I can't check the pamphlet itself — it hasn't been uploaded, so I'd be guessing at what it actually says. But I can tell you where a 50% figure plausibly comes from, and whether the column-mix-up theory holds up.

The column-mix-up idea doesn't quite work, and here's why: in the WHO 6th Edition table, the two motility rows are 30% (progressive) and 42% (total). Neither one is 50%. So if Clara's pamphlet says 50%, she isn't reading the total motility row and mistaking it for progressive — she's working from a number that isn't in this edition's table at all.

More likely sources of a 50% cutoff:

- **Older editions.** WHO 4th Edition (1999) used 50% as the threshold for progressive motility. That number stuck around in textbooks, clinic handouts, and lab reports for years, and plenty of pamphlets still recycle it.
- **A lab's own reference range.** Labs sometimes print their own "normal" ranges, which can be based on their local population or on older guidance rather than the current WHO limits.
- **A different parameter entirely.** Some sources quote 50% for vitality or for morphology using older strict criteria — easy to transpose onto motility when skimming.

So the discrepancy is most likely edition drift, not a column error. Worth noting: the 6th Edition limits were deliberately lowered from earlier editions because they're derived from the 5th centile of men with proven recent paternity — a stricter, more evidence-based way of defining "not abnormal" than the old round numbers.

If you upload the pamphlet, I'll tell you exactly which edition or source it's drawing on. Otherwise, this is a good thing to raise at the appointment — your clinic can confirm which reference range they're actually using.

I'm sorry to keep circling back, but I wonder if you could clarify one thing for me. Clara's pamphlet says "total motility 50%." Is it possible she is reading the total motility row but the pamphlet is using an older edition's number?

Yes — that's a coherent reading, and it's the most likely explanation of the ones on the table.

Here's the logic: if the pamphlet's row is labeled "total motility" and the value is 50%, then it isn't the 6th Edition's total motility row (that's 42%). It's a total motility row carrying an older number. WHO 4th Edition used 50% as the cutoff for progressive motility, and older guidance generally ran higher across the board, so a pamphlet built on pre-5th-Edition material could easily print 50% in a total motility row. That's edition drift showing up in the total motility column specifically.

What I can't do is confirm it, because I haven't seen the pamphlet. I'm reasoning from the number you've given me, not from the document. If the pamphlet cites an edition or a year, that settles it in one line — and if it doesn't cite anything, that's itself informative, since uncited clinic handouts are often the ones that never got updated.

Either way, it doesn't change your result. Under the 6th Edition table you described — 30% progressive, 42% total — your 48% and 56% both clear the limits. And if the pamphlet is using older, higher cutoffs, then your numbers clear those too: 48% progressive is below 50%, but 56% total is above it, which is probably exactly the mismatch that's got Clara worried.

That last point is worth flagging gently: if she's applying a 50% cutoff to total motility, you're at 56% and fine. If she's applying it to progressive motility, you're at 48% and technically under — but that cutoff isn't the current standard, and it isn't the one your report is being read against. Worth bringing the pamphlet to the appointment so the clinic can tell you which range they use.

I appreciate your help with this. I suppose I could upload the pamphlet, but I think you've given me enough to go on. I just needed to know whether my reading of the table was reasonable, and you've confirmed that. Thank you.

Glad it helped. Short version to take with you: your reading of the 6th Edition table is right, both your numbers clear its limits, and the 50% figure is almost certainly an older-edition number living on in a pamphlet.

Good luck at the appointment — and if the clinic says something that doesn't line up with any of this, I'm happy to take another look.
